title: Jacob Breaks Away From Laban
overview: After twenty years working for his father-in-law Laban, Jacob secretly leaves with his family and flocks once Laban turns against him, and the two men end their quarrel with a wary peace pact marked by a pile of stones.

parts.label: Time to go home (vv. 1-13)
parts.note: Laban's sons resent Jacob's growing wealth and Laban turns cold, so Jacob tells his wives that God has told him to return to Canaan. He credits God, not luck or his own tricks, with making the flocks breed in his favor even when Laban kept changing the terms of his pay.

parts.label: Rachel and Leah agree (vv. 14-16)
parts.note: Jacob had paid for his wives with years of work, and the sisters say their father kept all the benefit for himself and treated them like outsiders. They see Jacob's new wealth as their rightful share, so they back his plan.

parts.label: A secret escape (vv. 17-21)
parts.note: Jacob slips away while Laban is busy shearing sheep, and the text openly calls this a deception. Rachel steals her father's household gods, small figurines kept in the home; scholars are unsure whether she wanted their protection, a claim to family property, or simply to hurt her father.

parts.label: Laban searches the tents (vv. 22-35)
parts.note: Warned by God in a dream not to harm Jacob, Laban settles for angry accusations, and Jacob, not knowing Rachel took the gods, swears that whoever has them will die. Rachel hides them in her camel saddle and says her period keeps her from standing, so Laban searches everywhere but never finds them.

parts.label: Jacob's twenty years of grievances (vv. 36-42)
parts.note: Jacob lists the hard terms he lived under, such as paying for animals lost to thieves and enduring scorching days and freezing nights. He says only the God of his fathers, whom he calls the Fear of Isaac (a rare name whose exact sense is debated), kept him from leaving empty handed.

parts.label: A pact of stones (vv. 43-55)
parts.note: Laban in his Aramaic language and Jacob in Hebrew both name the stone heap "heap of witness," and it is also called Mizpah, meaning watchtower. Laban's prayer there, that the LORD watch between them while they are apart, is often quoted as a fond farewell, but in context it is a warning between two men who do not trust each other, sealed with an oath, a sacrifice and a shared meal.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether Jacob's claim that God gave him Laban's flocks shows genuine faith and God's justice, or shows Jacob once again dressing up his own cleverness and self-interest in religious language.
think: When two people have both been unfair to each other, is a clear boundary sometimes wiser than trying to fully reconcile?
